accepted.question_text: Over RCA0, are the following four statements equivalent: (A) the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for any finite number of trees; (B) Milliken's Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes; (C) the canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph; and (D) the statement that for every k >= 2, the Rado graph has the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings?

evidence.quote: The following implications are known as ZFC, or even just ZF, results: with (A) =⇒ (B) =⇒ (C) =⇒ (D).
(1) Are any of (A) - (D) equivalent over RCA0?

accepted.question_text: Is the reverse-mathematical strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for edges in the Rado graph strictly greater than the reverse-mathematical strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs of natural numbers?
accepted.context_brief: Rado graph edges versus pairs of naturals

evidence.quote: In [5], Dobrinen, Laflamme, and Sauer proved that the Rado graph has the rainbow Ramsey property.
(2) Is the rainbow Ramsey theorem for edges in the Rado graph strictly stronger than the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs on the natural numbers?

accepted.question_text: Fix any graph G with three vertices and any k >= 2. Assuming over RCA0 the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers, does it follow that every coloring of copies of G in the Rado graph into countably many colors, with each color used at most k times, has a subgraph isomorphic to the Rado graph in which no two copies of G receive the same color?
accepted.context_brief: Triples of naturals versus three-vertex graphs

evidence.quote: This means that fixing any finite graph G and k ≥ 2, given any coloring of all copies of G in R into ω many colors such that each color appears no more than k times, there is a subgraph R′ of R which is again a Rado graph, and such that no two copies of G in R′ have the same color.

(3) What about k-bounded colorings of graphs with three vertices in the Rado graph versus k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers? That is, assuming the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers, does the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of copies of G in the Rado graph follow over RCA0, where G is any graph on three vertices?

accepted.question_text: For each d, is the reverse-mathematical strength of the strong-tree version of the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for d trees strictly weaker than the corresponding strength for d + 1 trees?
accepted.context_brief: Halpern-Lauchli strength by number of trees

evidence.quote: (A) The Halpern-L¨auchli Theorem for any finite number of trees. This is a ZF theorem.
(4) Is the reverse math strength of the (strong tree version) Halpern-L¨auchli Theorem for d trees strictly weaker than for d + 1-trees?

accepted.question_text: For each d, is the reverse-mathematical strength of the strong-tree version of the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for d trees strictly stronger than the reverse-mathematical strength of the somewhere dense matrix form for d trees?

evidence.quote: (5) Is the reverse math strength of the strong tree version of Halpern-L¨auchli for d trees strictly stronger than the somewhere dense matrix form for d trees? (This would contrast with results in [3] (see also [4]), where we showed that these two forms are equivalent for strongly inaccessible cardinals, over ZFC.)

accepted.question_text: Does the statement that the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem holds for any finite number of trees have the same reverse-mathematical strength as the statement that Milliken's theorem for colorings of finite strong trees holds?

evidence.quote: (A) The Halpern-L¨auchli Theorem for any finite number of trees. This is a ZF theorem.
(B) Milliken’s Ramsey theorem for strong trees (on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes). It is proved by induction using the Halpern-L¨auchli Theo￾rem.
(6) Does “The Halpern-L¨auchli Theorem holds for any finite number of trees” have the same strength as “Milliken’s Theorem for colorings of finite strong trees holds”?

accepted.question_text: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of Milliken's theorem depend on the height of the finite strong trees being colored?

evidence.quote: (B) Milliken’s Ramsey theorem for strong trees (on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes). It is proved by induction using the Halpern-L¨auchli Theo￾rem.
(7) Does the strength of the Milliken Theorem depend on the height of the finite trees being colored?

accepted.question_text: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of either the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem or Milliken's theorem depend on the splitting properties of the underlying finitely branching trees; for example, are binary-branching trees weaker than ternary-branching trees, and are both weaker than trees whose branching is finite but unbounded?

evidence.quote: (8) Does the strength of either the Halpern-L¨auchli Theorem or the Milliken Theorem depend on the splitting properties of the trees? For instance, are two-branching trees weaker than three-branching trees,..., weaker than finitely but unboundedly branching trees?

accepted.question_text: What is the reverse-mathematical strength of the following statement: for every finite graph G and every k >= 2, every coloring of all copies of G in the Rado graph into countably many colors, with each color used at most k times, has a subgraph isomorphic to the Rado graph in which no two copies of G receive the same color?
accepted.context_brief: Strength of the Rado rainbow Ramsey property

evidence.quote: This means that fixing any finite graph G and k ≥ 2, given any coloring of all copies of G in R into ω many colors such that each color appears no more than k times, there is a subgraph R′ of R which is again a Rado graph, and such that no two copies of G in R′ have the same color.
(9) What is the Reverse Mathematics strength of the statement (D)?

accepted.question_text: For the Rado graph, does the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings have the same reverse-mathematical strength as the rainbow Ramsey property for (k + 1)-bounded colorings?

evidence.quote: This means that fixing any finite graph G and k ≥ 2, given any coloring of all copies of G in R into ω many colors such that each color appears no more than k times, there is a subgraph R′ of R which is again a Rado graph, and such that no two copies of G in R′ have the same color.
(10) Does the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings of the Rado graph have the same reverse math strength as for (k + 1)-bounded colorings?

accepted.question_text: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph coincide with the reverse-mathematical strength of Sauer's canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph?
accepted.context_brief: Rainbow theorem versus canonical partition theorem

evidence.quote: (C) Canonical partition theorem on colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph. (This implies that the Rado graph has finite big Ramsey degrees.)
(11) Does the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph have the same reverse math strength as the canonical partition theorem of Sauer?

accepted.question_text: When one colors copies of different finite graphs inside the Rado graph, do the resulting rainbow Ramsey theorems all have the same reverse-mathematical strength, or does that strength vary with the number of vertices in the finite graph being colored?
accepted.context_brief: Dependence on the finite graph being colored

evidence.quote: This means that fixing any finite graph G and k ≥ 2, given any coloring of all copies of G in R into ω many colors such that each color appears no more than k times, there is a subgraph R′ of R which is again a Rado graph, and such that no two copies of G in R′ have the same color.

(12) How do the strengths of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph compare for colorings of different finite graphs? Are they all the same, or does the number of vertices in the finite graph being colored affect the strength?
